back: Greet, take history, examine, order imaging or labs if needed, form a clinical impression, then explain findings and plan. History comes first because it decides which exam procedures to choose.

front: A patient says 'I have a herniated disc.' What is the chief complaint?
back: The symptom that brought the patient in, such as back pain for two weeks. The herniated disc claim is recorded separately as a diagnosis the patient reports, not as the chief complaint.

front: Why is 'It hurts more when you bend, right?' poor history technique?
back: It is a leading question. It suggests the answer and biases the reply. Start with open questions like 'Tell me about your pain,' then use focused closed questions to fill gaps.

front: Morning stiffness lasts over an hour in a young man with back pain. What does this suggest?
back: Inflammatory disease such as ankylosing spondylitis or rheumatoid arthritis. Stiffness under 30 minutes fits osteoarthritis instead.

front: A patient with back pain feels better leaning forward on a shopping cart. What condition fits?
back: Lumbar spinal stenosis. Bending forward opens the canal. Pain that gets worse with cough or Valsalva points more toward disc herniation.

front: Name the red flag: back pain at night that does not ease with any position.
back: Night pain unrelieved by position is a red flag for tumor or infection. Mechanical pain usually eases with rest or a change of posture.

front: A 70 year old man with prostate cancer history has new night back pain and lost 15 pounds in four months. Next step?
back: Imaging and lab work, and coordinate with his oncologist. Cancer history, weight loss and night pain together raise strong concern for bone metastasis, so do not just treat.

front: Which primary cancers most often spread to bone?
back: Breast, lung, prostate, kidney and thyroid. A history of any of these with new back pain is a red flag for metastasis.

front: Back pain plus saddle numbness, urinary retention and weak legs on both sides. What is it and what do you do?
back: Cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency. Refer immediately. Do not manipulate. Look for reduced anal sphincter tone and lost perianal sensation.

front: What do the CAGE questions screen for?
back: Alcohol problems. Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye opener. Two or more positive answers suggest a problem.

front: How much unexplained weight loss counts as a standard red flag?
back: More than about 10 pounds over six months. It points toward cancer, infection or a systemic disease.

front: Why can a blood pressure cuff that is too small mislead you?
back: It gives a falsely high reading. The cuff should cover about 80 percent of the arm circumference, with the patient seated, rested, and the arm at heart level.

front: What blood pressure difference between the two arms is abnormal, and what might cause it?
back: More than 10 to 15 mmHg. Think subclavian stenosis, aortic dissection or thoracic outlet compression. Take pressure in both arms at the first visit.

front: What counts as orthostatic hypotension?
back: A drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing. Common causes are dehydration, certain drugs and autonomic problems.

front: Which stage of hypertension is 130 to 139 over 80 to 89?
back: Stage 1 hypertension. Normal is under 120/80, elevated is 120 to 129 with diastolic under 80, and stage 2 is 140/90 or higher.

front: A hard, fixed, nontender lymph node sits above the left collarbone. What is it called and what does it suggest?
back: Virchow node. It suggests abdominal cancer. Soft, tender, mobile nodes suggest infection instead.

front: A 62 year old woman has gradual mid back pain unaffected by movement, nausea after fatty meals, and arrested breathing on pressure under the right rib margin. What next?
back: Murphy sign points to gallbladder disease. Refer her. Spinal manipulation is not the answer for referred visceral pain.

front: In what order is the abdomen examined and why?
back: Inspect, auscultate, percuss, then palpate. Listening comes before touch because palpation can change bowel sounds. Examine painful areas last.

front: Cullen sign and Grey Turner sign suggest what?
back: Hemorrhagic pancreatitis or retroperitoneal bleeding. Cullen is bluish color around the navel. Grey Turner is discoloration of the flank.

front: Compare lung findings: pleural effusion versus pneumothorax.
back: Effusion gives dull percussion with decreased fremitus and breath sounds. Pneumothorax gives hyperresonant percussion with decreased fremitus and breath sounds.

front: What does high sensitivity let you do when a test is negative?
back: Rule the condition out. High specificity lets you rule the condition in when the test is positive. A cluster of findings is more reliable than one sign.

front: Describe the plumb line in a lateral posture view.
back: It passes through the ear canal, middle of the shoulder, greater trochanter, slightly in front of the knee center, and slightly in front of the lateral malleolus.

front: In upper crossed syndrome, which muscles are tight and which are weak, as taught for the exam?
back: Tight: upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectorals. Weak: deep neck flexors and lower trapezius. It shows as forward head and rounded shoulders.

front: Lower crossed syndrome causes which pelvic and spinal posture?
back: Anterior pelvic tilt with increased lumbar lordosis. Hip flexors and erector spinae are tight, while abdominals and gluteals are weak.

front: How do you tell a structural scoliosis from a functional curve on the Adams test?
back: A structural curve shows a rib hump on the convex side when bending forward. A functional curve straightens. Cobb angle above about 10 degrees defines scoliosis.

front: How do you measure true leg length versus apparent leg length?
back: True: ASIS to medial malleolus. Apparent: umbilicus to medial malleolus, which suggests pelvic obliquity or contracture. A difference under 1 cm is common.

front: A patient's pelvis drops on the swing side. Which gait and which weak muscle?
back: Trendelenburg gait from weak gluteus medius on the stance side, often from superior gluteal nerve injury (L4 to S1). The trunk may lurch toward the weak side.

front: A patient lifts the knee high to clear the foot. Name the gait and nerve.
back: Steppage gait from foot drop. Think deep peroneal nerve or L4 and L5 involvement.

front: Which gait is wide based and worsens with eyes closed?
back: Sensory ataxic gait, which is the basis of the Romberg test. Cerebellar ataxia is also wide based, but swaying is not much worse with eyes closed.

front: Spurling's test reproduces arm pain. What does it indicate?
back: Cervical radiculopathy. The neck is extended and side bent toward the symptomatic side with downward pressure. Cervical distraction should relieve it if a root is compressed.

front: Which test is done by watching the radial pulse while the neck is extended and rotated and the patient inhales deeply?
back: Adson's test. A reduced pulse suggests scalene compression in thoracic outlet syndrome. Roos test uses three minutes of hand opening and closing in surrender position.

front: Straight leg raise causes leg pain below the knee at 45 degrees. Is it positive and what does it suggest?
back: Yes. Pain below the knee between about 30 and 70 degrees suggests disc herniation with L5 or S1 root irritation. Back or hamstring pain alone is not a positive test.

front: Which test is highly specific for disc herniation: pain on the symptomatic side when the opposite leg is raised?
back: The well leg raise (Fajersztajn or crossed straight leg raise). It usually indicates a medial herniation.

front: Which nerve roots does the femoral nerve stretch test assess?
back: L2 to L4. Anterior thigh pain during the prone knee bend is positive.

front: What is the Laslett cluster?
back: At least three positive sacroiliac provocation tests out of five: distraction, thigh thrust, Gaenslen, compression and sacral thrust. It raises the likelihood of sacroiliac joint pain.

front: Which test checks for a torn Achilles tendon?
back: Thompson's test. Squeezing the calf fails to produce plantar flexion when the tendon is ruptured.

front: Compare Apley's compression and distraction tests.
back: Compression hurting suggests a meniscus lesion. Distraction hurting suggests a ligament lesion.

front: A patient has a down and out eye, ptosis and a dilated pupil. Which cranial nerve?
back: Oculomotor, CN III. CN IV supplies the superior oblique and CN VI the lateral rectus. Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) is sympathetic instead.

front: Half of a patient's face is paralyzed including the forehead. Peripheral or central lesion?
back: Peripheral, such as Bell's palsy. A central upper motor neuron lesion spares the forehead because of bilateral cortical input.

front: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear and bone conduction beats air on Rinne. What type of hearing loss?
back: Conductive loss. In sensorineural loss, air still beats bone but both are reduced, and Weber lateralizes to the normal ear.

front: List the key myotomes from C5 to S1.
back: C5 shoulder abduction, C6 elbow flexion and wrist extension, C7 elbow extension and wrist flexion, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction, L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 plantar flexion.

front: Which test uses an ankle systolic over brachial systolic pressure and what value means arterial disease?
back: The ankle brachial index. Below 0.9 indicates peripheral arterial disease. Above 1.4 suggests calcified, noncompressible vessels.

front: What does a laboratory reference range actually represent?
back: The values found in about 95 percent of healthy people. So about 1 in 20 healthy people falls outside it on any one test. Always read the range printed on the report.

front: A urine dipstick is positive for blood but the sediment shows no red cells. What might it be?
back: Hemoglobin or myoglobin, as in rhabdomyolysis. Red cells in the sediment would confirm true hematuria.

front: Why does a negative nitrite not rule out a urinary infection?
back: Some organisms, such as Enterococcus, do not convert nitrate to nitrite. Positive nitrite suggests gram negative bacteria like E. coli.

front: Which urinary cast points to glomerulonephritis, and which to pyelonephritis?
back: Red cell casts mean glomerulonephritis. White cell casts mean pyelonephritis. Casts form in the tubules, so they place the problem in the kidney.

front: Alkaline urine is linked to which bacteria and stones?
back: Urea splitting bacteria such as Proteus, and struvite stones. Acidic urine goes with uric acid stones and ketoacidosis.

front: Numb feet, a smooth red tongue and high MCV. Which diagnosis?
back: Vitamin B12 deficiency, a macrocytic anemia. It can cause subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Iron deficiency is microcytic.

front: A shift to the left on a white cell count means what?
back: More immature neutrophils called bands, a sign of acute bacterial infection. Neutrophils normally make up about 55 to 70 percent of white cells.

front: What INR target applies to a patient on warfarin?
back: Usually 2.0 to 3.0. Higher values raise bleeding risk, which matters before manipulation. Platelets under about 50,000 are also a caution.

front: Which marker is a sensitive screen for lupus and which tests are more specific?
back: ANA is sensitive, over 95 percent positive, but not specific. Anti double stranded DNA and anti Smith are far more specific for lupus.

front: Which antibody is more specific than rheumatoid factor for rheumatoid arthritis?
back: Anti CCP. It may appear before erosions develop. Rheumatoid factor also shows up in lupus, Sjogren syndrome and some healthy older adults.

front: A patient has deep bone pain, ESR of 90, anemia, high calcium and punched out lytic spine lesions. Diagnosis and ALP?
back: Multiple myeloma. Alkaline phosphatase is often normal because the lesions are purely lytic. Confirm with protein electrophoresis. Manipulation is contraindicated.

front: Compare crystals in gout and pseudogout under polarized light.
back: Gout: needle shaped monosodium urate, negatively birefringent. Pseudogout: rhomboid calcium pyrophosphate, weakly positively birefringent, often in the knee with chondrocalcinosis.

front: A joint fluid white count is above 50,000 with low glucose and positive Gram stain. Which category?
back: Septic arthritis. It can destroy a joint within days, so urgent referral is needed. Inflammatory fluid is about 2,000 to 50,000.

front: An ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. What is the diagnosis and the action?
back: Inferior myocardial infarction (ST elevation in II, III and aVF). Call for emergency transport and do not adjust.

front: What do the five parts of acute angle closure glaucoma look like?
back: Painful red eye, blurred vision with halos, mid dilated nonreactive pupil, hard globe, and nausea or vomiting. It is an emergency.

front: A cherry red spot at the macula with a pale retina suggests what?
back: Central retinal artery occlusion, a stroke of the eye. Painless sudden vision loss in one eye is a vascular emergency.

front: A patient over 50 has new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and very high ESR. Diagnosis and risk?
back: Giant cell arteritis. Untreated, it can cause blindness, so urgent medical referral is needed.

front: A smoker has shoulder and arm pain, Horner syndrome and hand weakness. What tumor?
back: Pancoast tumor at the lung apex. It is easily mistaken for a cervical or shoulder problem.

front: How do you tell tension pneumothorax from simple pneumothorax?
back: Tension adds tracheal deviation away from the affected side, falling blood pressure and distended neck veins. It needs immediate treatment.

front: Chest pain is sharp, worse lying flat, better leaning forward, with a friction rub. Diagnosis?
back: Pericarditis. Aortic dissection instead gives sudden tearing pain to the back with unequal arm blood pressures.

front: Aortic stenosis murmur: describe its timing, site and radiation.
back: Systolic crescendo decrescendo at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids, with syncope, angina and dyspnea.

front: At what abdominal aortic aneurysm diameter is repair usually considered?
back: 5.5 cm or more. A pulsatile mass with sudden back or abdominal pain is a rupture until proven otherwise.

front: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, relieved by leaning forward, with high amylase and lipase. Diagnosis?
back: Pancreatitis. Common causes are alcohol and gallstones. Pain worse with eating suggests gastric ulcer, while food relieves a duodenal ulcer.

front: Sudden severe scrotal pain, high riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex. Diagnosis and urgency?
back: Testicular torsion, a surgical emergency within hours. Epididymitis builds gradually and may improve when the testis is lifted.

front: A young woman has a missed period, pelvic pain and one sided tenderness. What must be considered early?
back: Ectopic pregnancy, a surgical emergency. Consider pregnancy early in any woman of childbearing age with pelvic pain.

front: What does Courvoisier sign suggest?
back: Jaundice with a painless, palpable gallbladder suggests cancer of the pancreatic head.

front: A diabetic patient has a stocking pattern of sensory loss. What is the cause?
back: Diabetic neuropathy. Fasting glucose of 126 or higher, or A1c of 6.5 or higher, is diagnostic of diabetes.

front: A 45 year old has low back pain to the lateral calf and top of the foot, weak great toe extension, normal reflexes. Which root and likely disc?
back: L5 radiculopathy, probably from an L4 to L5 herniation. Lost ankle reflex with weak plantar flexion would instead point to S1.

front: Name the six setup elements graded at the Part IV Technique Station.
back: Patient position, doctor position, segmental contact point, doctor's contact point, stabilization hand, and line of drive. You must show and say each one aloud so the grader can give credit.

front: What is a high velocity, low amplitude (HVLA) thrust?
back: A fast, shallow, short lever thrust given at the end of the joint's passive range, often after a pre load takes out the slack.

front: What is the segmental contact point, and how is it different from the doctor's contact point?
back: The segmental contact is the bony part of the patient you touch, like a mammillary process. The doctor's contact is the part of your own hand that touches, like the pisiform.

front: A patient has a sudden severe headache and neck pain after a minor bump. Adjust or refer?
back: Refer. This could be cervical artery dissection. The history carries the most weight, and rotation tests alone are unreliable as a screen.

front: Which condition is a surgical emergency and an absolute contraindication to adjusting the region: cauda equina syndrome or osteoporosis?
back: Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, bladder or bowel loss, both legs weak). Osteoporosis is only relative, so you use low force or non thrust methods.

front: Give four absolute contraindications to HVLA at the involved region.
back: Fracture, malignancy of the spine, spinal infection, unstable ligament injury or instability, cauda equina syndrome, progressive neurologic deficit, or suspected vascular injury. Any four of these are right.

front: Is anticoagulation therapy an absolute or relative contraindication to adjusting?
back: Relative. You may change the technique or force, or defer, while the condition is managed. Others in this group are osteoporosis, hypermobility and active inflammatory arthritis.

front: In the cervical spine below C2, lateral flexion and rotation go to which sides relative to each other?
back: The same side (ipsilateral coupling), because of the way the facets are angled.

front: In the lumbar spine in neutral, how do rotation and lateral flexion couple (Fryette type I)?
back: Rotation goes to the opposite side of the lateral flexion. In flexion or extension (type II), they go to the same side.

front: Which cervical joint gives about half of neck rotation?
back: The atlantoaxial joint (C1 to C2), turning through the odontoid. The atlanto occipital joint mostly does nodding, flexion and extension.

front: What is the order of barriers when a joint is moved past active range?
back: Physiological barrier, then the elastic barrier, then the paraphysiological space, then the anatomical limit. An adjustment goes into the paraphysiological space but never past the anatomical limit.

front: Is an audible pop needed for a successful adjustment?
back: No. The pop (cavitation) is gas bubble formation in synovial fluid. Success depends on restoring joint motion, not on the sound.

front: What segmental contact is used to adjust the atlas (C1)?
back: The transverse process, found just below the mastoid and behind the ramus of the mandible. The atlas has no body or spinous process.

front: What is the segmental contact for the axis (C2)?
back: The large bifid spinous process or the lamina.

front: In a supine cervical rotational adjustment of C3 to C7, what is the segmental contact?
back: The articular pillar of the restricted segment. The doctor stands at the head of the table and uses a small, quick thrust along the facet plane.

front: At what point in breathing is a prone thoracic thrust usually given?
back: At the end of exhalation. The patient breathes out and you thrust at the end, with a posterior to anterior line of drive.

front: Which ribs are typical, and which are atypical?
back: Typical ribs are 3 to 9. Atypical ribs are 1, 2, 10, 11 and 12. Ribs 1 to 7 are true, 8 to 10 false, and 11 and 12 floating.

front: A rib is restricted in inhalation. Is it described as elevated or depressed?
back: Depressed. An elevated rib is restricted in exhalation.

front: Describe the side posture lumbar roll: segmental contact and line of drive.
back: Contact the mammillary process (or spinous process) with the pisiform or index web. The line of drive is posterior to anterior and slightly inferior to superior, with rotation through the segment.

front: Is flexion distraction a thrust technique? When is it a good choice?
back: No, it is a gentle non thrust option. It is useful for disc involvement and spinal stenosis, or when thrust is relatively contraindicated.

front: For a posterior ilium (PI) in side posture, what is the segmental contact and line of drive?
back: Contact the ischial tuberosity, and drive anterior and superior along the SI joint line. The drive moves the ilium opposite to its listed misplacement.

front: A patient fell on an outstretched hand and has wrist pain. Which carpal bone is most often fractured, and what comes before manipulation?
back: The scaphoid. Rule out fracture first, before any wrist manipulation. The lunate is the classic carpal dislocation.

front: What are the three phases of tissue healing and their rough timing?
back: Inflammatory (first 72 hours), proliferative or repair (about day 3 to week 6), and remodeling (about week 3 to a year or more).

front: A freshly sprained ankle needs which kind of modality, heat or cold?
back: Cold with compression. Heat in acute injury increases bleeding and swelling. Heat is for subacute and chronic stiffness.

front: What does PRICE stand for?
back: Protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation. It is the classic protocol for acute injury, with cold used in the first 48 to 72 hours.

front: What are the usual application times for a hot pack and for an ice pack?
back: Hot pack about 15 to 20 minutes with toweling between pack and skin. Ice pack about 10 to 20 minutes, and ice massage 5 to 10 minutes.

front: Name three conditions where cold therapy is contraindicated.
back: Raynaud's disease, cold urticaria, cryoglobulinemia, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, impaired circulation or sensation. Any three are right.

front: Which ultrasound frequency goes deeper, 1 MHz or 3 MHz, and how deep?
back: 1 MHz goes deeper, about 3 to 5 cm. 3 MHz stays superficial, about 1 to 2 cm. Lower frequency goes deeper.

front: Why use pulsed ultrasound instead of continuous?
back: Pulsed ultrasound (like 20 percent duty cycle) gives nonthermal effects such as cavitation and streaming. It is chosen when heating is unwise, as in acute injury.

front: What is the difference between phonophoresis and iontophoresis?
back: Phonophoresis uses ultrasound to drive a topical drug through the skin. Iontophoresis uses direct current to drive charged ions in.

front: Under which pole is negatively charged dexamethasone placed for iontophoresis?
back: The negative pole, since like charges repel and push the drug into the tissue.

front: What beat frequency do interferential currents of 4,000 Hz and 4,100 Hz produce?
back: 100 Hz, the difference between the two. Two medium frequency currents cross in the tissue to make a low frequency effect.

front: Which TENS setting works by the pain gate, and which is thought to release endorphins?
back: High frequency, low intensity TENS (about 80 to 120 Hz) uses the pain gate. Low frequency, high intensity TENS (about 2 to 5 Hz) is thought to release endorphins.

front: A patient has a demand type pacemaker. Is electrical stimulation safe?
back: No. Implanted electronic devices are a contraindication, along with use over the carotid sinus, anterior neck, chest, pregnant abdomen and impaired skin.

front: Vitamin D deficiency causes what in children, and what in adults?
back: Rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Vitamin D helps calcium absorption and bone mineralization.

front: A patient takes warfarin. Which vitamin must stay steady, and why?
back: Vitamin K, because it is needed for clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Swings in intake change how well warfarin works.

front: A strict vegan has numbness and macrocytic anemia. Which vitamin is low, and what is the condition?
back: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia with neuropathy, from dietary lack. True pernicious anemia is the same picture caused by missing intrinsic factor.

front: Which exercise program do the McGill big three form?
back: A core endurance program for the low back: the curl up, the side bridge and the bird dog. They build endurance while limiting spinal load.

front: Upper crossed syndrome: which muscles are tight, and which are weak?
back: Tight: upper trapezius, levator scapulae, pectorals. Weak: deep neck flexors, lower trapezius, rhomboids, serratus anterior. The result is forward head and rounded shoulders.

front: What should you do if exercise makes leg pain move farther from the spine (peripheralization)?
back: Stop and reassess. Increasing radicular symptoms or progressing neurologic signs during exercise are signs to stop.

front: How many stations are in the new Part IV, and what are they?
back: Eight: seven Patient Encounter stations and one Technique station. They replace the older 25 short stations.

front: What is the timing of one Patient Encounter station?
back: 2 minutes to read the chart at the door, 14 minutes with the simulated patient (a maximum), and 6 minutes to type the SOAP note.

front: What three things do you do with the simulated patient?
back: Take a focused case history, perform a focused exam, and give a brief report of findings in plain words.

front: Name the five grading domains of each Patient Encounter.
back: Patient Evaluation, Patient Examination, Clinical Decision Making and Case Management, Interpersonal and Communication Skills, and Documentation.

front: Which grading domain judges your case history?
back: Patient Evaluation, which is obtaining relevant clinical information. Relevant is the key: five sharp questions beat ten random ones.

front: Which domain is where you decide to treat, co manage or refer urgently?
back: Clinical Decision Making and Case Management. Red flags matter most here.

front: What are the three kinds of cases mixed into every Part IV session?
back: Treatable in a chiropractic office, needs more testing or co management, and needs urgent referral or is outside scope.

front: Which seven body systems do Part IV cases come from?
back: Musculoskeletal, neurological, cardiovascular and pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocrine, renal and urological, and malignant.

front: What does OLDCARTS stand for?
back: Onset, Location, Duration, Character, Aggravating factors, Relieving factors, Timing, Severity. It guides a focused history of a pain complaint.

front: Why should you narrate your exam out loud, including the side?
back: The encounter is video recorded, and the grader needs to hear what you did and found. Naming left or right avoids costly side errors.

front: What are the cauda equina warning signs in a back pain encounter?
back: Loss of bladder or bowel control, saddle numbness, and weakness in both legs. This patient needs emergency referral to the emergency department now.

front: A 58 year old has night mid back pain, weight loss of 8 kg and past prostate cancer. What is your plan?
back: No spinal adjustment. Urgent referral to a medical doctor for imaging and workup, since spinal metastasis is possible, and explain why in plain words.

front: Chest pain with sweating, nausea and spread to the jaw or arm in a diabetic smoker. What do you do?
back: Send the patient to an emergency department. Possible heart attack is a cardiovascular red flag, so this is an emergency referral.

front: A patient with back pain also has burning urination, fever and flank pain. What might it be?
back: A kidney infection, not a spine problem. Ask about urine in every back pain case, and refer for medical care.

front: A patient has great thirst, frequent urination, tiredness and blurry vision. Which type of case is this likely?
back: Possible new diabetes. It is usually a co manage or test further case, needing tests and a medical provider.

front: What does SOAP stand for?
back: Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan. It is the standard way clinicians write down a visit.

front: What belongs in the Objective part of a SOAP note?
back: Vital signs, inspection, palpation, range of motion, and each test with its result and side. Write the finding, such as SLR positive on the right at 40 degrees, not just the test name.

front: Why is Right lumbar sprain and strain, no nerve root signs, a better assessment than back pain?
back: It is specific. It names the likely condition, the side, and what you ruled out. Vague assessments lose points.

front: What is the rule for the Plan section of a SOAP note?
back: It must match the assessment. List treatment, home advice, follow up time, tests or imaging, and any referral with how urgent it is.

front: List three common SOAP note mistakes.
back: Left and right errors, missing red flags, a plan that does not match the assessment, vague assessment, a test name with no result, facts never found, or a note so long you never reach the plan.

front: How long is the Technique station, and how many adjustments do you set up?
back: 14 minutes to set up ten chiropractic adjustments. You show and say the setup but do not thrust hard on a person.

front: Give a good order for saying any technique setup aloud.
back: Name the target level and side, then patient position, doctor position, segmental contact, doctor's contact, stabilization, line of drive. Using the same order each time builds a habit.

front: Name common errors at the Technique station.
back: Wrong contact point, a line of drive that does not fit the contact, forgetting the stabilization hand, silent setups, poor doctor position, and rushing or lingering.

front: What is teach back, and why use it in a Part IV encounter?
back: After explaining your plan, ask the patient to say it back in their own words. It checks understanding and shows good communication.

front: What should you do before touching the simulated patient or moving a drape?
back: Ask consent. Introduce yourself, explain what you will do, and ask permission again before any uncomfortable step or undressing.
